content: A glucose tolerance test is a diagnostic procedure in which glucose is administered to evaluate how efficiently it is cleared from the bloodstream. This test is primarily used to diagnose diabetes, assess insulin resistance, and occasionally to investigate reactive hypoglycemia. The glucose is typically administered orally, making the most common form of this test the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). It may also be included as part of a broader diagnostic panel, such as the comprehensive metabolic panel. Patients are advised not to restrict carbohydrate intake in the days or weeks leading up to the test, as this could affect the results. The test should not be conducted during an illness, as the results may not accurately reflect the patient’s glucose metabolism under normal, healthy conditions. For individuals weighing less than 43 kilograms (94 pounds), a full adult dose of glucose should not be administered, as this could lead to exaggerated glucose levels and potentially false-positive results. For the OGTT, the patient must fast for 8 to 14 hours prior to the test, although water is permitted. The test is typically scheduled in the morning (between 7:00 and 8:00 AM) because glucose tolerance follows a diurnal rhythm, with reduced tolerance observed in the afternoon. A baseline blood sample is collected at the start of the test. The patient is then given a glucose solution to drink, containing 75 grams of glucose (or 1 gram per kilogram of body weight, up to a maximum of 75 grams). This solution must be consumed within five minutes. Historically, a 100-gram dose was used prior to 1975. Blood samples are subsequently collected at specific intervals to measure glucose levels, and sometimes insulin levels, depending on the purpose of the test. For basic diabetes screening, the most critical samples are the fasting (baseline) and 2-hour post-glucose samples, which may be the only ones collected. In research settings, additional samples may be taken at various time points. If renal glycosuria (sugar in the urine despite normal blood glucose levels) is suspected, urine samples may also be collected alongside the fasting and 2-hour blood tests. Diagnostic thresholds for diabetes include a fasting blood glucose level of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or higher, and a 2-hour post-glucose level of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or higher. Impaired glucose tolerance is indicated by a 2-hour glucose level between 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) and 11.0 mmol/L (199 mg/dL). A standard 2-hour OGTT is generally sufficient to diagnose or rule out all forms of diabetes mellitus, except in the earliest stages of disease development. Extended versions of the test have been used for other purposes, such as identifying reactive hypoglycemia or characterizing subsets of hypothalamic obesity. Insulin levels may also be measured during the test to evaluate insulin resistance or deficiency. However, the OGTT has limited utility in diagnosing reactive hypoglycemia because normal results do not exclude the condition, abnormal results do not confirm that symptoms are related to the test findings, and many asymptomatic individuals may exhibit late glucose drops that are considered characteristic of reactive hypoglycemia. In this context, the OGTT is often used to support a diagnosis that is already suspected based on other evidence, but it is insufficient on its own to confirm or refute the diagnosis, unlike its use in diagnosing diabetes. When glucose is administered intravenously, the procedure is referred to as an intravenous glucose tolerance test (IVGTT). This method has been employed to investigate early abnormalities in insulin secretion in prediabetic states.
